paper_title: MULTI3IR: A Benchmark for Multi-perspective Multi-domain Multi-modal Information Retrieval

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Information retrieval (IR) increasingly targets open-ended queries that admit diverse perspectives. Existing IR benchmarks, however, focus primarily on closed-ended queries, while even open-ended benchmarks largely consist of queries whose supporting documents span a single subject domain and modality. We introduce Multi$^3$IR, a benchmark that evaluates how well retrievers cover the multifaceted perspectives of open-ended queries across diverse domains and modalities. It comprises 104.9K Stack Exchange queries, each annotated with perspective descriptions that capture the query's implicit viewpoints. We further propose SPIN, a parameter- and label-efficient method that learns noise vectors to steer embeddings toward diverse yet meaningful semantic directions. Experiments show that existing multimodal retrievers suffer from single-perspective bias, while SPIN substantially improves perspective coverage on Multi$^3$IR and generalizes well to unseen open-ended IR benchmarks. The dataset and experimental code are available at https://github.com/seokwon99/Multi3IR.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Information retrieval (IR) has expanded from factoid queries to open-ended queries that decompose into perspectives, complementary sub-queries that each capture distinct facet. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1, the query Why are so few foods blue? implicitly raises perspectives such as Why are blue pigments so rare in nature? and How are blue foods generally perceived by people? These perspectives provide information from diverse subject domains (e.g., biology, psychology) and modalities (e.g., text, image), collectively contributing to more comprehensive answer. Recent efforts have advanced open-ended IR in several directions. On the evaluation side, some benchmarks (Min et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2024; Figure 1: datapoint example of MULTI3IR. An openended query includes multiple implicit perspectives (three in this example), each paired with supporting documents from different domains and modalities. Chen and Choi, 2025) incorporate open-ended queries that admit multiple answers grounded in different documents. On the method side, retrieval diversification, including query expansion (Gao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a) and multi-vector retrieval (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Humeau et al., 2019), seek to cover diverse aspects of query rather than relying on single dominant interpretation. However, current approaches remain limited in two key respects. First, as shown in Table 1, most IR benchmarks focus on closed-ended queries, overlooking information needs where quality depends on comprehensiveness or diversity. Even open-ended benchmarks largely consist of queries grounded in single-domain, text-only documents, leaving it unclear whether retrievers can provide comprehensive information across heterogeneous knowledge sources. In this paper, we introduce MULTI3IR, an openended IR benchmark comprising 104.9K queries collected from Stack Exchange. For each query, we annotate set of perspectives, each represented as sub-query paired with the documents that support it. As shown in Table 1, each query in our benchmark requires comprehensive information spanning 3.34 domains and 1.91 modalities on average. We further propose SPIN, parameterand label-efficient IR training method that learns noise vectors to diversify the output of frozen retriever into multiple perspective-aware embeddings, without requiring costly document-level annotations. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We propose MULTI3IR, large-scale benchmark of 104.9K open-ended queries that require comprehensive information across multiple subject domains and modalities. 2. We identify single-perspective bias in current multimodal retrievers, where retrieval for an open-ended query concentrates on few dominant perspectives while neglecting the rest. 3. We propose SPIN, parameterand labelefficient training method that achieves higher perspective coverage than existing diversification methods.

sections.title: 2.1 Open-ended Information Retrieval
sections.content: Open-ended IR benchmarks examine whether retriever can gather documents covering diverse information needs within question. Early work such as AmbigQA (Min et al., 2020) introduced questions with multiple valid interpretations, with each disambiguation grounded in Wikipedia documents, but evaluates question answering rather than retrieval. PIR (Zhao et al., 2024) extends this setting to retrieval, evaluating whether retriever can return documents relevant to an explicitly specified perspective within query. Since users rarely state their perspectives, BeRDS (Chen and Choi, 2025) instead gives the retriever only the original question and evaluates whether the retrieved documents cover all annotated perspectives. However, these benchmarks largely consist of queries grounded in single-domain, text-only documents, limiting their ability to evaluate comprehensive retrieval across diverse knowledge sources. MULTI3IR addresses this gap by collecting supporting documents across multiple domains in both text and image modalities.

sections.title: 2.2 Retrieval Diversification
sections.content: Dense retrievers rank documents by similarity to single query vector, which cannot be close to all relevant documents when they are scattered across the embedding space (Chen et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2025). Prior work introduces diversity at three stages. Post-retrieval re-ranks an initial candidate pool to promote diverse results (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998; Kulesza and Taskar, 2012); since they only reorder the first-stage pool, documents missing from it remain unretrievable. Query expansion rewrites the query before retrieval, generating hypothetical documents (Gao et al., 2023) or pseudo-answers (Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a), at the cost of an LLM call for every query. Multi-vector retrieval represents query with multiple embeddings (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Humeau et al., 2019), expanding the regions it can cover, but training them relies on costly document-level relevance annotations, especially for open-ended queries spanning multiple perspectives. SPIN addresses this by training multivector retriever using only perspective descriptions, improving perspective coverage without documentlevel annotations or query-time LLM inference. sections.title: 3.2 Dataset Construction
sections.content: As illustrated in Figure 2, we construct the dataset using an automated three-stage pipeline. After that, we conduct human annotation to construct test set. Overall dataset statistics are presented in Figure 3. Selecting posts. We collect posts from Stack Exchange, rich source of multi-answer threads with diverse perspectives. We use 77 sites across five categories, retain posts with more than 3 answers, and sample uniformly across categories. For each post, is the concatenated title and body, and is the set of answers. See Appendix B.1 for details. Perspective extraction and verification. We extract perspectives ˆP = {ˆp1, ˆp2, . . .} from using GPT-5-mini, then verify them as follows: 1. Uniqueness. We encode all perspectives with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) and discard any ˆpj whose maximum cosine similarity to ˆP {ˆpj} exceeds 0.8. 2. Faithfulness. We use Bespoke-MiniCheck7B (Tang et al., 2024) to produce binary entailment judgment between each ˆpj and A, and discard any ˆpj judged as not entailed. We remove questions with fewer than four perspectives, yielding 104.9K questions and 521.7K perspectives. See Appendix B.2 for details. Document retrieval and verification. We collect documents supporting each perspective from two sources: Google Image Search for images and the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4) (Raffel et al., 2020) for text. Using each ˆpi as query, we retrieve the top-10 documents from each and define ˆDi as their union. Since retrieved documents may support multiple perspectives, we enforce exclusive support: using Qwen3-VL-30BA3B-Instruct (Team, 2025), we verify each ˆd ˆDi against ˆpi and the other perspectives, and define Di as those supporting ˆpi alone. Finally, we label each document in Di with subject domain using EAI-Distill-0.5b (AI et al., 2025), yielding 1.01M multimodal documents with 3.34 domains and 1.91 modalities per query on average. See Appendix B.3 for retrieval and verification details, and Appendix for domain labeling.

sections.title: 4.1 Preliminary Analysis
sections.content: Open-ended queries often admit multiple perspectives, yet whether existing retrievers adequately capture such diversity remains unclear. We investigate this on our test set using three multimodal retrievers: MM-Embed-8B (Lin et al., 2024), GMEQwen2-VL-7B-Instruct (Zhang et al., 2024b), and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B (Li et al., 2026). Do retrievers cover multiple perspectives? We first examine perspective coverage (Figure 4(a)). Given the original query, we retrieve the top 20 documents and check whether at least one supporting document is retrieved for each perspective. We find that retrieval is heavily concentrated on single dominant perspective, while the remaining ones receive substantially lower scores, revealing single-perspective bias. Where does the bottleneck originate? We next ask whether the bias stems from the query embedding failing to capture other perspectives or from poor alignment between the query and the document embeddings of their supporting documents (Figure 4(b)). When we instead use perspective descriptions as queries and aggregate the results via Round Robin, the previously missed documents become retrievable, yielding substantially more balanced performance across perspective ranks. This indicates that the bottleneck lies in the query embedding rather than the document space, motivating perspective-guided learning with multiple query vectors aligned to explicit perspective descriptions. sections.title: 4.2 Perspective-Guided Learning
sections.content: mized noise vector at layer l: To enable the retriever to interpret queries in diverse ways, we propose SPIN (Steering Perspectives by Injecting Noise), which requires only perspective descriptions and no document relevance annotations. Prior work (Skean et al., 2024, 2025) shows that intermediate transformer layers preserve richer semantic information, whereas the final layers converge toward single fixed interpretation. Motivated by this, SPIN injects learnable noise vectors at an intermediate layer of frozen retriever to steer its embeddings toward diverse perspectives. Optimization process. We describe the optimization procedure in Algorithm 1. For each query qn, we inject each learnable noise vector ε into the hidden representation of qn at layer and forward it through the remaining layers, yielding the steered embeddings Sn. We then encode the perspective descriptions Pn with the same frozen encoder into target embeddings Tn, and optimize so that Sn aligns with Tn. Since both Sn and Tn consist of multiple vectors, aligning the two sets requires many-to-many optimization. Rather than imposing fixed one-toone assignment (e.g., Hungarian matching (Kuhn, 1955)), we formulate alignment as probabilistic coverage problem. Specifically, each Sn independently produces coverage probability for target Tn, and these probabilities are combined via noisy-OR, so that is considered covered if at least one aligns with it. The positive loss Lpos encourages every Tn to be covered by any Sn, whereas the negative loss Lneg requires all Sn to reject in-batch negatives from other queries, T=n. Inference. (4) At each round = 1, 2, . . . , we iterate through (Re1, . . . , Rem) in order and append the rank-r document of each list to Rq, skipping duplicates. The procedure terminates once Rq = k.

sections.content: We evaluate perspective coverage using two metrics. Hard coverage checks whether the retrieved documents include any annotated supporting document for each perspective, offering reproducibility and scalability. Since our annotations may miss relevant documents, soft coverage uses GPT-5-mini to assess whether each retrieved document supports given perspective, recovering evidence that hard coverage would treat as miss. sections.title: 5.2 Baselines
sections.content: We experiment with several retrieval diversification methods on three state-of-the-art multimodal retrievers: GME-Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct (Zhang et al., 2024b), MM-Embed-8B (Lin et al., 2024), and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B (Li et al., 2026). For multi-vector retrieval methods (m > 1), results are aggregated via round robin. We use 72K instances as the training set and 32K as the validation set, and document embeddings remain frozen throughout. See Appendix C.3 for implementation details. Naive. We evaluate the retrievers in both zeroshot and fine-tuned ways. For fine-tuning, we concatenate positive documents across all perspectives per query into single positive set, and train the retriever with in-batch negatives using InfoNCE (Oord et al., 2018). LLM-Expansion. We diversify the query space by prompting an LLM with the instruction Generate {m} search queries related to: {user_query} to obtain distinct query reformulations. To adapt the model to our setting, we fine-tune Qwen34B (Team, 2025) to generate the annotated perspective descriptions corresponding to each query, where is set to the number of annotated perspectives during training. At inference time, we fix = 5 for consistency across queries. Auto-Regressive Embedding (ARE). We implement the ARE method (Chen et al., 2025; Huo et al., 2026) in our setting, which generates multi-vector embeddings auto-regressively. During training, the retriever takes the query tokens followed by supporting document embeddings and produces one query embedding per position. The query embeddings are aligned with gold documents via Hungarian matching, and InfoNCE is applied with in-batch negatives. At inference, we fix = 5 and perform sequential forward passes. ARE cannot be applied to the encoder-based retriever MM-Embed, so we exclude it from the experiments. SPIN. We inject learnable noise vectors at an intermediate layer to steer final-layer embeddings, requiring only perspective descriptions without document relevance annotations. To account for different backbone depths, we set the injection point at = 0.5L, corresponding to layers 16, 14, and 18 for MM-Embed (L = 32), GME-Qwen2 (L = 28), and Qwen3-VL (L = 36), respectively. See 4.2 for details. Oracle. We use oracle perspective descriptions as retrieval queries, serving as an upper bound for perspective-guided retrieval.

sections.content: Current retrievers capture information from limited perspectives. We examine the zero-shot performance of naive retrievers on MULTI3IR. They reach only up to 28.83 HC@10 and 39.52 SC@10, leaving substantial gap to the oracle setting where the perspective descriptions are explicitly provided. Providing these perspectives boosts performance by 15.58 to 35.31 points on HC@10 and by 31.28 to 36.72 points on SC@10, suggesting that current retrievers struggle to identify perspectives that are only implicit in query. The gap persists even at = 100, with difference of 19.45 to 35.60 points on HC@100, indicating that the failure is not one of retrieval depth but of query understanding. How the retriever learns matters more than what it learns from. We compare methods within each level of supervision. Under documentlevel supervision, ARE improves over the finetuned naive retriever by 5.30 to 6.20 points on HC@10. Under perspective-level supervision, the gap widens: SPIN outperforms LLM-EXPANSION by 8.18 to 13.13 points on HC@10 and by 17.99 to 21.92 points on SC@10, despite using the same annotations and the same number of query embeddings. Notably, multiple query embeddings alone provide no benefit, as LLM-EXPANSION falls below the naive baseline on HC@10 while also using = 5. Multi-vector retrieval helps only when the embeddings are explicitly trained to align with distinct perspectives, indicating that the architecture

Perspective-guided learning boosts retrieval with lighter annotation effort. We compare ARE and SPIN, two multi-vector retrievers trained with document-level and perspective-level supervision, respectively. As shown in Table 2, SPIN outperforms ARE by 3.62 to 4.47 points on HC@10 and by 14.47 to 14.62 points on SC@10, demonstrating that perspective-level alignment is more effective than document-level supervision for training multi-vector retrievers. Perspective-level supervision is also substantially cheaper to obtain, as document relevance annotation dominates the overall synthesis cost (Appendix B.5). Perspectiveguided learning is thus both more effective and lighter to annotate, offering more scalable path toward training perspective-aware retrievers.

sections.title: 5.4 Results on Other Benchmarks
sections.content: We report zero-shot retrieval performance on two unseen open-ended IR benchmarks, PIR (Zhao et al., 2024) and BeRDS (Chen and Choi, 2025), in Table 3. Since both provide perspective-level gold documents, we measure HC@k by strict document match, without judge model. Each query is encoded from the original question alone, and the perspectives are never shown to the retriever. Further details on the benchmark subsets and corpora are in Appendix C.2. SPIN improves over the naive retriever across all three backbones on both benchmarks. On PIR, the gains range from 9.37 to 11.73 points on HC@10 and remain substantial at k=100 (3.81 to 6.09 points). On BeRDS, where the naive retrievers already achieve high coverage, the gains are smaller for MM-EMBED and QWEN3-VL but reach 20.10 points on HC@10 for GME-QWEN2, which has the lowest naive coverage. The only exception is MM-EMBED at HC@100 on BeRDS, where both methods exceed 98%, leaving little room for improvement. Overall, these results show that perspective-aware steering learned on MULTI3IR transfers to unseen benchmarks with different domains and corpora, without adaptation to the target distribution.

sections.title: 6 Analysis
sections.content: All experiments in this section are conducted with Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B (Li et al., 2026), which has 36 layers in total. Implementation details, including the training configuration and the retrieval instructions, follow Section 5.3.

sections.title: 6.1 Effect of Injection Layer
sections.content: A central mechanism of SPIN is to inject noise into an intermediate layer of the retriever. As shown in Table 4, injecting at the mid layer (L=18) yields consistent improvements as increases. In contrast, late-layer injection (L=30) plateaus as increases, likely because the representations at deeper layers have already collapsed toward single direction. These results suggest that intermediate-layer injection is essential for SPIN to fully benefit from increasing m.

sections.title: 6.3 Knowledge Source Coverage
sections.content: To quantify how well SPIN retrieves information across diverse knowledge sources spanning modalities and domains, we compare it with zero-shot naive baseline and an oracle upper bound. As shown in Table 6, SPIN nearly saturates the oracle on modality coverage, reaching 78.2 versus 81.1 at k=100 and closing 91% of the naive-to-oracle gap. In contrast, SPIN closes only 3547% of the naive-to-oracle gap for domain coverage, and the shortfall persists as grows (68.3 versus 84.8 at k=100). Learning domain-aware steering vectors is promising direction for closing this gap.

sections.title: Positives
sections.content: Prior work identifies limitation of dense retrievers: single query vector may not be close to all relevant documents when they are scattered across the embedding space (Chen et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2025). To examine whether SPIN is effective for such dispersed queries, we analyze performance by document dispersion. As shown in Table 7, SPIN yields its largest gains on dispersed queries (+24.4 HC@100 at m=5 for the top quartile), while also improving substantially on tightly clustered queries (+8.7).

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduce MULTI3IR, an openended IR benchmark of 104.9K queries from Stack Exchange, annotated with perspective descriptions and supporting documents. We further propose SPIN, parameterand label-efficient method that learns lightweight steering vectors to diversify frozen retrievers output into multiple perspectiveaware embeddings, using only perspective descriptions. Our experiments show that strong multimodal retrievers suffer from single-perspective bias, collapsing onto one dominant viewpoint. SPIN substantially mitigates this bias, outperforms document-supervised baselines with lighter annotation, and generalizes to external benchmarks. Further analysis reveals that the bias persists even when relevant documents are tightly clustered in the embedding space, and that injecting steering vectors at an intermediate layer is critical to SPINs effectiveness.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We acknowledge several potential limitations of our work. (1) The number of perspectives can vary substantially across queries, while our method uses fixed number of perspective vectors m. Developing an adaptive mechanism that selects based on each query is promising direction for future work. (2) While SPIN reduces the need for documentlevel annotations, jointly leveraging perspective descriptions and their supporting documents during training could further improve perspective-specific (3) Finally, MULTI3IR is constructed retrieval. through an automatic pipeline involving perspective extraction, document retrieval, and exclusivesupport verification. Although we validate this pipeline both quantitatively and qualitatively, LLMinduced biases may not be fully eliminated and could affect the absolute scores reported in our evaluations.

sections.title: A Subject Domain Classification
sections.content: We annotate each documents subject domain using the domain classifier1, text classification model that assigns label from two-level taxonomy of 10 top-level classes, each divided into 10 subclasses, for 100 domains in total  (Table 8)  . Since the classifier accepts only text input, image documents require textual surrogate. For WebQA, we use the caption paired with each image; for MultimodalQA, the title of the Wikipedia page from which the image is drawn; and for M-BEIR and MRMR, caption generated by an image captioning model2. Since every document in Multi3IR originates from web source, we crawl the source page for each image and use its textual content. Each input is truncated to the models 512-token context window, and the domain with the highest predicted probability is assigned.

sections.title: B Data Collection Details
sections.content: B.1 Raw Data Collection We use the official StackExchange data dumps hosted on archive.org3. Although the dataset is publicly available, it may contain user-generated content such as usernames, posts, and comments that could include personally identifying or offensive information. The authors checked all examples and found no personally identifying information (PII). We select this source for three reasons: (1) the multi-answer structure provides natural multiperspective supervision, (2) community voting and accept-tagging serve as built-in quality control, and (3) external links cited in answers serve as natural source of perspective-grounded evidence. We collect data from 77 sites organized into 5 broad categories: technology, culture & recreation, science, business, and life & arts. Some sites appear in multiple categories under the multicategory specification (e.g., graphic_design belongs to both technology and life & arts). For each site, we retain question only if it has more than three answers and receives votes from more than three distinct users, ensuring both quantity and diversity of viewpoints. For each retained post, the question is formed by concatenating the title and body, and the answer set is the aggregation of all user responses. To avoid over-representation of dominant categories such as technology, we then apply category-level uniform sampling with percategory cap. Per-category counts at each stage with representative sites are reported in Table 9. B.2 Perspective Extraction and Verification We extract perspectives using GPT-5-mini (gpt-5mini-2025-08-07) via the OpenAI Batch API; the prompt and an example are shown in Figure 5. For uniqueness, we encode perspective summaries with the sentence-transformers library4 and iteratively remove perspective whose cosine similarity to any previously kept perspective exceeds the threshold; the threshold of 0.8 was chosen through manual inspection to best separate near-duplicates from genuinely distinct perspectives. For faithfulness, we concatenate the entire answer set into single document and use it as the supporting document, and run the entailment check via the minicheck library5 on vLLM backend6 with prefix caching. The per-category distribution after both filters is reported in Table 10. B.3 Document Retrieval and Verification We use Qwen3-Embedding-4B7 served via vLLM to encode both the query and the C48 English documents with 4,096-token context window. Queries are prefixed with Instruct: Given web search query, retrieve relevant passages that answer the querynQuery:{query}, while documents are encoded without any prefix. Image candidates are obtained from the Google Images endpoint of the Serper API9. To verify whether each document exclusively supports its assigned perspective, we prompt VLM using the template in Figure 6. We evaluate three models under two criteria: (i) fully-only, which accepts only fully support predictions, and (ii) fully+partially, which also accepts partially support. The former shows higher agreement with human judgments, while Qwen3-VL-30B-A3BInstruct10 achieves the best precision and recall. 4https://www.sbert.net/ 5https://github.com/Liyan06/MiniCheck 6https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm 7https://huggingface.co/Qwen/ 1https://huggingface.co/EssentialAI/ Qwen3-Embedding-4B eai-distill-0.5b 2https://huggingface.co/Salesforce/ blip-image-captioning-large 8https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/c4 9https://serper.dev/ 10https://huggingface.co/Qwen/ 3https://archive.org/details/stackexchange Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct

Completions API11 with reasoning_effort=medium and max_completion_tokens=2000. The judge is given single perspective and one retrieved document at time, and produces chain-of-thought followed by verdict of fully, partially, or not supported; only fully is counted as positive. The judge prompt is shown in Figure 6. To assess the reliability of the judge, we further measure its agreement with human annotators on held-out sample of 100 perspective-document pairs, balanced across domains and modalities. We binarize the ratings into fully supported and not supported, where the latter includes both partially and not supported. Human annotators achieve substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss κ = 0.743), while the GPT-5-mini judge shows even stronger agreement with the human majority vote (Fleiss κ = 0.840). These results indicate that the judges decisions closely align with human judgments. C.2 Details on Other Benchmarks PIR. We use all six sub-datasets of PIR (Zhao et al., 2024), comprising 4,187 questions and 10,019 perspectives. Each question is retrieved against its own corpus, and every perspective carries its own relevance judgments, so no subset selection is needed. BeRDS. BeRDS (Chen and Choi, 2025) is designed to be scored by judge model over retrieved passages rather than against gold documents, and only its ArguAna subset provides perspective-level document annotations. The Kialo and OpinionQA subsets define perspectives but leave them unanno11https://platform.openai.com/docs/ api-reference/chat C.3.1 Base retriever. All methods for fine-tuning retrievers share the same instruction prompt, Retrieve images or text relevant to the users query. All resulting embeddings are L2-normalized. Document embeddings are precomputed once and remain frozen. The main results are reported from single run. For GME-Qwen2-VL12 and Qwen3-VLEmbedding13, the instruction and the query are wrapped with the Qwen2-VL chat template14, producing <im_start>systemn{instruction}<im_end> <im_start>usern{query}<im_end> <im_start>assistantn<endoftext> Both are causal decoders, and we take the hidden state at the last token position as the query embedding. uses For MM-Embed15, which bidirectional attention, we instead concatenate the Instruct: instruction and the query as {instruction}nQuery: {query} following its original convention, and obtain the query embedding via the models latent-attention pooling head, which aggregates the full sequence of hidden states through learned attention layer. C.3.2 Fine-tuning All fine-tuned methods are trained on the same 72K queries sampled from MULTI3IR with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) using cosine schedule with 3% warmup. Method-specific details are described below. Naive (fine-tuned). We fully fine-tune the retriever using InfoNCE with in-batch negatives (temperature τ =0.05), with learning rate of 1e5 and batch size of 32 for 3 epochs. The maximum query length is set to 512 tokens. 12https://huggingface.co/Alibaba-NLP/ gme-Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct 13https://huggingface.co/Qwen/ Qwen3-Embedding-8B 14https://huggingface.co/Qwen/ Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct/blob/main/chat_template. json 15https://huggingface.co/nvidia/MM-Embed LLM-Expansion. We fully fine-tune Qwen34B16 on (query, perspective description) pairs with learning rate of 2e5 for 2 epochs using cosine schedule with 3% warmup. The effective batch size is 16 (batch size 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps). At inference, we generate m=5 query reformulations per query using HuggingFace transformers17 with AutoModelForCausalLM.generate, with temperature= 0.7, top-p = 0.8, top-k = 20, and maximum of 384 tokens. ARE. We fine-tune the retriever with LoRA (r=16) and an additional input projection layer Win RHH (H=3584 for GME-Qwen2VL, H=4096 for Qwen3-VL-Embedding; Xavierinitialized, without bias) that maps document embeddings into the language-model input space, using learning rate of 3e5, an effective batch size of 32. Predicted query embeddings are aligned to gold document embeddings via Hungarian matching, and the matched pairs are trained with InfoNCE over in-batch negatives with temperature τ =0.01 for Qwen3-VL-Embedding and τ =0.03 for GME-Qwen2-VL. SPIN. We optimize noise vectors ϵ RmH injected into the mid layer (layer 18 of 36 for MM-Embed and Qwen3-VL-Embedding, layer 14 of 28 for GME-Qwen2-VL), with all encoder weights frozen. We set m=5, yielding 20,480 trainable parameters for MM-Embed and Qwen3VL-Embedding (H=4096) and 17,920 for GMEQwen2-VL (H=3584). The noise vectors are initialized from (0, 0.012). Learning rates are tuned per backbone: 3e4 for MM-Embed, 1e2 for Qwen3-VL-Embedding, and 1e3 for GMEQwen2-VL. We use batch size of 32. The training objective is the noisy-OR loss described in 4.2, where each similarity is converted into probability via p(d) = σ((sim b)/τ ) with τ =0.1 and b=0.5 fixed across all backbones. C.3.3 Computational Resources All experiments are run on NVIDIA A6000 48GB GPUs (Intel Xeon Silver 4210R CPU). Naive (finetuned) is trained with 4 GPUs using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)18, and LLMExpansion is trained with 4 GPUs using the TRL 16https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B 17https://github.com/huggingface/transformers 18https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/fsdp.html SFTTrainer19 (which wraps HuggingFace Trainers Distributed Data Parallel). ARE, SPIN, and zeroshot evaluation are run on single GPU.

sections.content: AI-assisted coding tools were used to support data analysis and visualization, including drafting and debugging scripts for figure/table generation. All code and results were subsequently reviewed and validated by the authors. 19https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer PerspectiveDocument Supportedness Judge Prompt You are judging whether document supports answering specific perspective. Follow this reasoning process: 1. Identify what the perspective specifically asks for. 2. Describe what the document actually contains only what is literally visible. Do NOT assume or infer content. 3. Compare the two and give verdict. Verdicts: fully: The document explicitly contains the specific answer the perspective asks for. partially: The document has related information but does not fully answer the specific question. not: The document is only topically related or unrelated, with no specific answer. Output constraints: Combine steps 13 into one paragraph inside <reason> tags. The verdict must be exactly one of: fully, partially, or not, inside <verdict> tags. In-context examples Example 1. < reason > The perspective asks for method to spatially join point data to polygon attributes in QGIS . The document shows the QGIS " Join Attributes by Location " dialog [...]. This is the exact tool needed to perform the spatial join . </ reason > < verdict > fully </ verdict > Example 2. ... Example 3. ... Example 4. ...
